title: Construct 2D Grid Matching Graph Layout
statement:
An undirected graph has `n` nodes labelled `0` to `n - 1`, and each `edges[i] = [u, v]` joins nodes `u` and `v`. Place the nodes in a rectangular grid (a list of rows that all have the same length) so that:

- every node from `0` to `n - 1` occupies exactly one cell, and
- two nodes sit in side-by-side cells (left and right, or above and below) exactly when an edge joins them.

The input always allows such a layout. Return the grid as a 2D array. Several layouts can work (mirror images and rotations, for example); any valid one is accepted.
constraints: The edges can always be laid out as a grid as described
notes:
## Intuition

A corner cell has the fewest neighbours: 2, or 1 when the grid is a single row. From one corner, the nearest other corner ends one full side of the grid, and the only shortest path to it runs straight along that side, so a BFS that stops at the first corner it meets yields the first row. After that nothing is left to choose: each node of a complete row has exactly one unplaced neighbour, the one directly below it, so the rest fills in row by row. (Backtracking over every shape also works, but only for tiny grids.)

## Approach

1. Build adjacency lists `graph` from `edges`.
2. Pick `start`, a node of the smallest degree, and keep that degree as `cornerDegree`.
3. BFS from `start`, recording `parent`; the first discovered node of degree `cornerDegree` is `end`.
4. Follow `parent` from `end` back to `start` to collect `firstRow`.
5. Mark `firstRow` as `seen`. While `grid` has fewer than `n` cells, build the next `row`: under each node of the last row put its only unseen neighbour, `below`.
6. Return `grid`.

## Example 1, step by step

The edges form the cycle 0-1-3-2-0, so every degree is 2: `start = 0` and `cornerDegree = 2`. The BFS from 0 discovers 1 first, whose degree is 2, so `end = 1` and `firstRow = [1, 0]`. Under 1 goes 3 and under 0 goes 2, giving `[[1, 0], [3, 2]]`. LeetCode shows `[[3,1],[2,0]]`, a rotation of it; both are accepted.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + m) for `m = edges.length`: every node and edge is handled a constant number of times.
- Space: O(n + m) for `graph`, `parent`, `queue`, `seen` and `grid`.

## Pitfalls

- A single row's corners have degree 1, not 2; taking the smallest degree covers both cases.
- With two rows, a node on a long side and its partner across both have degree 3, so "walk along the degree-3 border" is ambiguous. Stopping at the nearest corner avoids this: the first row becomes a short side.
- Stop the BFS at the first corner found; the opposite corner is not on the same side.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `graph` | adjacency lists |
| `start`, `end` | the starting corner and the nearest other corner |
| `cornerDegree` | a corner's degree (1 for a single row, otherwise 2) |
| `parent` | BFS parent of each discovered node, `-1` if undiscovered |
| `queue`, `head` | the BFS queue and its read position |
| `firstRow` | the side from `end` to `start` |
| `seen` | nodes already placed |
| `grid`, `row`, `below` | the rows so far, the row being built, and the node placed under `node` |
